title: How much of the big square is shaded?
description: A big square is cut into four equal squares, and a diamond is drawn in one of them. The corner triangles left over are measured against the small square first, and then against the big square by multiplying. Keeko thinks the two quarters should be added.
teaching_notes: One idea: a fraction of a small square is a fraction of a fraction of the big square, so the two fractions are multiplied. Watch for students who add the two quarters instead of multiplying them.

source: A big square is split into four equal squares. In the top-left square a diamond is drawn with corners at the middles of the sides, and the four corner triangles are the part left over. Two corner triangles, the ones on the right, are shaded. What fraction of the big square is shaded?
video_script.why: A learner sees that a shaded part inside a small square is a fraction of a fraction of the big square, found by multiplying.
video_script.substitution: the book's own big square cut into four equal squares, with a diamond drawn in one of them
video_script.anchor: a big square cut into four equal squares, with a diamond drawn in the top left square and two corner triangles shaded
video_script.wrong_move: adds the two quarters, one quarter of the big square and one quarter of the small square, instead of multiplying them
video_script.payoff_line: One sixteenth of the big square is shaded.

final_answer.spoken: one sixteenth of the big square

video_script.fraction_reading: one quarter, half, one eighth, one sixteenth
maths_rules: each small square = 1/4 of the big square
diamond = 1/2 of the small square, so the four corner triangles = 1/2 of the small square
each corner triangle = 1/4 x 1/2 = 1/8 of the small square
two corner triangles = 2 x 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4 of the small square
shaded part = 1/4 x 1/4 = (1 x 1)/(4 x 4) = 1/16 of the big square
video_script.design: The big square on the left; the top left square is lifted out and enlarged, so the corner triangles can be seen against the small square before they go back into the big one.

<bookmark mark='tri'/>The four corner triangles share the other half equally.
<bookmark mark='each'/>Each triangle is one quarter of that half, which is one eighth of the small square.

<bookmark mark='mult'/>One times one over four times four.
